title: Hera hung from heaven
greek: ἄκμονας ἧκα δύω (akmonas hēka duō), 'I let down two anvils'
short: Zeus threatens Hera by recalling how he once hung her in the sky with anvils on her feet, to punish her persecution of Heracles.
body: Woken on Ida and seeing Hector vomiting blood, Zeus reminds Hera of an older punishment: he strung her up between sky and clouds, a golden bond on her wrists and two anvils tied to her feet, and hurled from Olympus any god who tried to free her (compare Hephaestus' fall, 1.590-4). Her offence was to raise a storm, with the North Wind's help, that drove Heracles to Cos as he sailed home from his own sack of Troy; Sleep has just told the same story at 14.249-62, and Apollodorus (2.7.1) retells it. Ancient critics were uneasy: Zenodotus left out 18-31 altogether, and Leaf thinks the internal evidence, including late word-forms, 'strongly in his favour'. Leaf notes that an anvil is simply the largest mass of metal early people handled, and so a handy instrument of torture, though Curtius proposed that the word here means thunderbolts; Leaf adds that Hesiod's akmōn at Theog. 722 might mean thunderbolt but more probably means an anvil. A scholiast even reports extra lines claiming the anvils were later dropped at Troy and shown to visitors.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.18-31, 15.19 and 15.21.
Apollodorus, Library 2.7.1 (Hera's storm, Heracles at Cos, Hera hung from Olympus).
Homer, Iliad 14.249-62 (Sleep's version of the same story).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἄκμων (thunderbolt; anvil).

title: Hera's oath by the Styx
greek: Στυγὸς ὕδωρ ... ὅρκος δεινότατος (Stygos hydōr ... horkos deinotatos)
short: Hera swears the gods' most binding oath, by the water of Styx, that Poseidon did not act at her wish: literally true, and deeply misleading.
body: The oath has a fixed form: Earth, Heaven and the 'down-flowing water of Styx' are called as witnesses, the gods' 'greatest and most dread oath'. Hesiod explains why it is dreaded: a god who forswears it lies breathless for a year and is shut out of the gods' councils for nine more (Theog. 775-806). Hera swore the same way to Sleep at 14.271-9, and Calypso to Odysseus (Od. 5.184-6). Here she adds Zeus' own head and their marriage bed. The art lies in what the oath does not cover. As Leaf points out, she speaks 'the truth so far': Poseidon did join the battle on his own initiative. But it was Hera's seduction of Zeus that gave him the chance, and Sleep went to tell Poseidon so (14.354-60). Zeus smiles (15.47); he seems to see through the oath and does not care, because he means to finish his own plan anyway.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.41 (Hera speaks the truth 'so far').
Hesiod, Theogony 775-806 (Styx and the penalty for a false oath).
Homer, Iliad 14.271-9 and Odyssey 5.184-6 (the same oath formula).

title: Zeus foretells the rest of the war
greek: Ἴλιον αἰπὺ ἕλοιεν Ἀθηναίης διὰ βουλάς (Ilion aipy heloien Athēnaiēs dia boulas)
short: Zeus lays out the plot to come: Patroclus will die, Hector will fall to Achilles, and Troy will be taken through Athena's plan.
body: This is the clearest statement in the poem of the 'plan of Zeus' (Dios boulē, 1.5). Zeus foretells, in order, Hector's rally, the flight to Achilles' ships, Patroclus' going out and killing Sarpedon, Patroclus' death at Hector's hands, Hector's death to avenge him, and finally the fall of Troy 'through the counsels of Athene', meaning the Wooden Horse, which Odysseus later calls the horse Epeius made 'with Athena' (Od. 8.493). He then ties the whole sequence back to his promise to Thetis in Book 1 (1.524-7). Alexandrian critics found the speech un-Homeric: Aristophanes and Aristarchus athetized 56-77, and Zenodotus omitted 64-77 as being 'like a Euripidean prologue'. Leaf agrees the objections to 64-71 are 'decisive'. Many modern readers value it all the same, because it shows the audience the shape of the coming books, so that what follows is watched as tragedy and not as suspense.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.56-77 and 15.71 (athetesis; Athena and the Wooden Horse).
Homer, Odyssey 8.492-5 (the Wooden Horse made by Epeius with Athena).
Homer, Iliad 1.5 and 1.524-7 (the plan of Zeus; his nod to Thetis).

anchor: darteth the mind of a man
title: Simile of the travelling mind
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἂν ἀΐξῃ νόος ἀνέρος (hōs d' hot' an aixēi noos aneros)
short: Hera flies as fast as thought: like a widely travelled man who wishes himself 'here or there' and is there in his mind at once.
body: Most Homeric similes compare things that can be seen: lions, storms, fire, waves. This one compares Hera's flight to the speed of a thought. A man who has travelled widely thinks 'would I were here, or there', and in imagination he is already there. Leaf calls it 'curious' and the only Homeric illustration drawn from 'purely mental processes'. The nearest parallels are the Phaeacian ships that are swift 'as a wing or a thought' (Od. 7.36), and a line in the Hesiodic Shield (222). Apollonius of Rhodes imitated the image (Argonautica 2.541-8). The point of comparison is speed, but the simile also fits Hera's state of mind: she is full of plans and wishes as she leaves Zeus to stir up trouble on Olympus.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.80 and 15.82.
Homer, Odyssey 7.36 (ships swift as a wing or a thought).
Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 2.541-8 (imitation of the simile).

title: Themis
greek: Θέμιστι καλλιπαρῄῳ (Themisti kallipareiōi)
short: Themis, 'Right Order', the goddess who presides over assemblies and the proper running of the feast, is the first to greet the shaken Hera.
body: Themis is the personification of themis, what is customary, ordained and fitting. In Homer she has a practical job. She calls and dismisses assemblies of men (Od. 2.68-9), and at the start of Book 20 Zeus tells her to summon all the gods to council (20.4-6). Hesiod makes her Zeus' second wife and mother of the Seasons and the Fates (Theog. 901-6). So it fits that Themis meets Hera with the welcome cup, and that Hera asks her to begin 'the equal feast': she is the guardian of the gods' good order. Hera then uses that order to stir up unrest. Her speech, which seems to counsel submission while inciting the gods, is called by Leaf a 'masterpiece worthy of Mark Antony'. The goddess of right order thus hosts the scene in which Ares almost breaks it.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.87 and 15.101-4 (Hera's speech compared to Mark Antony's).
Homer, Iliad 20.4-6; Odyssey 2.68-9 (Themis and assemblies).
Hesiod, Theogony 901-6 (Themis, mother of the Horae and Moirai).

title: Hera's laugh 'with her lips'
greek: ἣ δὲ γέλασσε χείλεσιν, οὐδὲ μέτωπον ... ἰάνθη (hē de gelasse cheilesin, oude metōpon ... ianthē)
short: A forced smile: Hera's lips laugh while her brow stays dark, an early piece of facial description that shows a gap between expression and feeling.
body: Homer rarely describes faces in detail, so this brief picture stands out. Hera 'laughed with her lips, but her forehead above her dark brows relaxed not'. Leaf compares the suitors' unnatural laughter 'with the jaws of others' (Od. 20.347) and observes that a forced smile is easier for the lips than for the eyes and brow. The detail shows that her calm is an act. She tells the gods to accept 'whatsoever evil thing' Zeus sends, and then, as if in passing, mentions that Ares' son Ascalaphus is dead (13.518-25). The remark is meant to provoke, and it works: Ares jumps up to take revenge. Compare her very different smile at 1.595-6, after Hephaestus has calmed the quarrel in Book 1, and her smile as she plots the seduction of Zeus (14.222-3).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.101 and 15.104.
Homer, Odyssey 20.345-9 (the suitors' unnatural laughter).
Homer, Iliad 13.518-25 (death of Ascalaphus).

anchor: avenge the slaying of my son
title: Ares and the death of Ascalaphus
greek: Δεῖμόν τε Φόβον τε (Deimon te Phobon te), 'Terror and Rout'
short: Told that his son Ascalaphus has fallen, Ares arms to avenge him in defiance of Zeus; Athena strips off his armour and talks him down.
body: Ascalaphus, who with his brother led the Minyans of Orchomenus (2.511-15), was killed by Deiphobus at 13.518-25. That passage pointedly says Ares had not yet heard the news, and Leaf thinks it was composed to prepare for this scene. Ares slaps his thighs, a Homeric gesture of grief and vexation also used by Patroclus at 15.397 and Achilles at 16.125. He tells Terror and Rout (Deimos and Phobos) to yoke his horses. These are his attendants and in Hesiod his children (Theog. 933-6). Athena saves the gods from Zeus' anger by taking away Ares' helmet, shield and spear, a small comic reversal of an arming scene. Her argument is a hard one: better men than his son have died and will die, and no one can save every mortal's line. Zeus himself will soon have to accept the same truth about Sarpedon.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.110, 15.113 and 15.119.
Hesiod, Theogony 933-6 (Phobos and Deimos, children of Ares).
Homer, Iliad 2.511-15; 13.518-25 (Ascalaphus).

title: The division of the world by lot
greek: τριχθὰ δὲ πάντα δέδασται, ἕκαστος δ' ἔμμορε τιμῆς (trichtha de panta dedastai, hekastos d' emmore timēs)
short: Poseidon protests that he, Zeus and Hades drew lots for sea, sky and underworld, so Zeus has no right to order an equal about.
body: Poseidon's angry reply gives the clearest Greek account of how the sons of Cronos shared the world. They shook lots: Poseidon won the grey sea, Hades the murky darkness, Zeus the broad sky, while earth and Olympus stayed common to all. Each 'got his share of honour' (emmore timēs), so in Poseidon's eyes Zeus is only the holder of 'his third portion'. Apollodorus repeats the story of the lots (1.2.1). Walter Burkert has pointed to a close Near Eastern parallel: in the Babylonian Atrahasis epic the gods Anu, Enlil and Enki also cast lots for heaven, earth and the deep. The episode shows a tension that runs through the poem. Zeus' rule rests on superior force and his rights as eldest (15.165-6, 182), while the other gods appeal to a fair division of honour (timē). Iris answers with the Erinyes who protect the elder-born, and Poseidon gives way.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.185-93.
Apollodorus, Library 1.2.1 (the sons of Cronos cast lots for sky, sea and underworld).
Walter Burkert, The Orientalizing Revolution: Near Eastern Influence on Greek Culture in the Early Archaic Age (Harvard University Press, 1992), pp. 88-91, on Iliad 15.187-93 and the Atrahasis epic.

title: Erinyes, guardians of the elder-born
greek: πρεσβυτέροισιν Ἐρινύες αἰὲν ἕπονται (presbyteroisin Erinyes aien hepontai)
short: Iris warns Poseidon that the Erinyes, the avenging Furies, always side with the elder brother, and Zeus is the elder.
body: Elsewhere in the Iliad the Erinyes punish wrongs within the family: a father's curse on his son (9.454), a mother's curse (9.571-2, 21.412), and perjury (19.259-60). Here they guard the order of birth. Leaf compares the respect due to elder brothers at 13.355 and explains the verb: the Erinyes 'attend' the elder as servants ready to come when called. Hesiod made Zeus the youngest son of Cronos, but the Iliad calls him the elder (15.166, 182), which strengthens his claim. Iris' gentle hint persuades Poseidon where threats failed. He praises a messenger with 'an understanding heart' (15.207), a line Pindar quotes as from Homer (Pythian 4.277-8). These Erinyes are not yet the snake-haired pursuers of Aeschylus' Eumenides. They are powers that enforce rights and obligations.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.204 and 15.207 (Pindar's quotation).
Homer, Iliad 9.454, 9.571-2, 19.259-60 (other Erinyes).
Pindar, Pythian 4.277-8.

title: Apollo and the aegis
greek: αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν (aigida thyssanoessan), 'the tasselled aegis'
short: Zeus lends his aegis to Apollo, who shakes it in the Greeks' faces and panics them: a weapon of pure terror.
body: The aegis (literally 'goatskin') is Zeus' shield or cape, made by Hephaestus 'for the putting to rout of warriors' (15.308-10). It is fringed and shaggy and causes terror. Usually Athena carries it (2.446-9, 5.738-42), but here Zeus lends it to Apollo, who has it again only in Book 24. LSJ lists this passage for the aegis 'lent to Apollo'. As long as Apollo holds it still, men on both sides fall evenly. When he looks the Danaans in the face, shakes it and shouts, their courage melts, and Homer pictures them as cattle scattered at night by two wild beasts. Leaf thinks lines 229-30 may have been added to explain why Apollo has the aegis at 308. In Book 24 Apollo again wraps the aegis around Hector, this time to protect his body from Achilles' abuse (24.18-21). The aegis shows the god's favour visibly, and it now belongs to the Trojans.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.229-35 and 15.308.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. αἰγίς (the skin shield of Zeus; lent to Athena and to Apollo).

title: The stalled horse simile (repeated from Book 6)
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος (hōs d' hote tis statos hippos)
short: Hector, revived, runs back to battle like a stalled horse that breaks its halter, the very simile used of Paris at the end of Book 6.
body: These six lines repeat word for word the simile in which Paris, in shining armour, runs down from Troy to rejoin Hector (6.506-11): a well-fed horse breaks its tether and gallops, head high and mane streaming, to the river and the mares' pastures. Aristarchus athetized 265-8 here and Zenodotus rejected only 265. Leaf holds that the simile loses much of its force when applied to Hector's speed alone instead of Paris' vain beauty, and he suspects the whole passage 263-305, yet he also remarks that the simile helps to bridge a gap in the narrative of Hector's return. Others defend it. In an oral tradition repeated similes are normal, and the repetition may carry meaning. Hector, who scolded Paris for idling, now takes on his brother's exuberant energy, but that energy comes from a god's breath and not from his own strength. Virgil admired the simile and used it for Turnus arming (Aeneid 11.492-7).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XV (on 263-305) and apparatus to 15.263-8 (Aristarchus' athetesis).
Homer, Iliad 6.506-11 (the simile first used of Paris).
Virgil, Aeneid 11.492-7 (imitation, of Turnus).

title: Exile after homicide
greek: ἄνδρα κατακτὰς γνωτὸν μητρυιῆς (andra kataktas gnōton mētryiēs)
short: Medon lives far from home because he killed a kinsman of his stepmother: in the Homeric world a killer usually fled abroad and lived as a dependant.
body: Medon, Oïleus' illegitimate son, killed a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, so he settled at Phylace in Thessaly (also 13.694-7). Books 15 and 16 are full of such men. Lycophron, Aias' squire, killed a man on Cythera and came to live with Aias (15.430-2). Epeigeus killed a kinsman and came to Peleus and Thetis as a suppliant (16.571-4). Patroclus himself came to Peleus as a boy after killing a playmate over a game of knucklebones (23.85-90). Homeric society had no state prosecution: the dead man's family took vengeance or accepted blood-price (9.632-6), so a killer fled and lived as a dependant of a foreign lord. Priam's entry into Achilles' hut is compared to the arrival of such a fugitive (24.480-2). These short biographies remind listeners that the men dying here had pasts, and that the epic often makes exiles into loyal followers.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 9.632-6 (blood-price, poinē, accepted for a slain brother or son).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. μητρυιά (stepmother; Il. 13.697).

title: Denial of burial
greek: οὐδέ ... γνωτοί τε γνωταί τε πυρὸς λελάχωσι θανόντα (oude ... gnōtoi te gnōtai te pyros lelachōsi thanonta)
short: Hector threatens any Trojan who hangs back: his kin will not give him 'his share of fire', and dogs will tear his body before the city.
body: Cremation by one's family was a dead man's 'due' or 'portion' (the Greek verb means 'to give a share of'). It allowed the spirit to pass into Hades (23.71-6), and to be left for dogs and birds was the worst disgrace a warrior could suffer. The theme is set in the poem's opening lines (1.4-5) and grows as the story goes on: Hector threatens the body of Patroclus (17.126-7, 18.175-7), Achilles threatens and tries to dishonour Hector's body (22.335-54), and the whole poem ends with Hector's funeral (24.782-804). Here a Trojan commander threatens his own men with the punishment otherwise kept for enemies, which shows how desperate the moment is. Compare Agamemnon's similar threat to Greek shirkers at 2.391-3. Sarpedon's burial in Book 16, granted by the gods, is the opposite of this threat.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. λαγχάνω (causal reduplicated aorist λελαχεῖν, 'give someone his portion' of fire; Il. 15.350).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.60 (λελαχεῖν in causal sense).

title: The boy and the sandcastle
greek: ὡς ὅτε τις ψάμαθον πάϊς ἄγχι θαλάσσης (hōs hote tis psamathon pais anchi thalassēs)
short: Apollo knocks down the Greek wall as easily as a child at the seashore kicks over the sandcastle he has just built.
body: The Achaean wall and trench, built in Book 7 (7.436-41) and fought over through Book 12, are the Greeks' great labour. Apollo kicks the trench banks into a causeway as wide as a spear-cast and then knocks the wall down as a boy, having made playthings in his childishness, 'confounds' them again with hands and feet. The simile measures the gap between divine and human effort, and it has an ironic poignancy, since the Greeks' 'long toil and labour' is turned into a child's game. The narrator speaks directly to the god, 'so lightly didst thou, O archer Phoebus', one of several moments in these books where the poet addresses a character. The scene also recalls 12.17-33, which tells how Apollo and Poseidon will wash the wall away entirely after the war. The sand of the simile anticipates that later effacement by the sea.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 7.436-41 and 12.17-33 (building and destruction of the wall).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.356 (Zenodotus' variant and Aristarchus on the god's 'dignity').
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἄθυρμα (plaything; Il. 15.363).

title: Nestor's prayer and the ambiguous thunder
greek: μέγα δ' ἔκτυπε μητίετα Ζεύς (mega d' ektype mētieta Zeus)
short: Zeus thunders in answer to Nestor's prayer, but the Trojans read the sign as theirs and attack harder: an omen that cuts both ways.
body: Nestor lifts his hands to the starry sky and reminds Zeus of the thigh-pieces burned to him 'in wheat-bearing Argos' by men praying for a safe return. This is the normal Greek logic of prayer: past offerings create a claim on the god. Zeus answers with a thunderclap, apparently a favourable sign, yet 'when the Trojans heard the thunder' they press on harder. Leaf notes that the omen seems to 'miss its mark' and to produce the opposite of its intended effect. One reading is that Zeus is in fact keeping both promises. He will save the Greeks in the end (15.69-71), but for now his favour is with Hector until a ship burns. Signs in the Iliad are often ambiguous in this way, and the people who interpret them hear what they want to hear: compare the eagle and snake omen that Hector rejects at 12.200-50.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XV (on the omen at 379) and note on 15.372 ('even in Argos').
Homer, Iliad 12.200-50 (Polydamas and the bird omen).

title: Pikes for sea-fighting
greek: ξυστοῖσι ... ναύμαχα κολλήεντα (xystoisi ... naumacha kollēenta)
short: The Greeks defend their beached ships from the decks with long boarding-pikes, the only naval weapons in Homer.
body: The fighting has now reached the ships, and the defenders climb onto the decks and use the long 'ship-fighting' poles (naumacha xysta) stored there. At 15.677-8 Aias swings one 'jointed with rings, of a length two and twenty cubits', about ten metres. Leaf explains kollēenta as 'glued' together from several lengths so that the joints are staggered, which makes a long shaft strong. He notes these are the only references to sea-fighting in Homer, though a seafaring people must have fought at sea. Since Homeric ships seem to have had no beaks for ramming, such pikes would have been used to fend off or board an enemy ship. The scene shows how far the Greeks have fallen: an invading army that came to besiege a city is now itself under siege at its own ships.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.388-9 and 15.677-8.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ναύμαχος ('pikes for sea-battles', Il. 15.389, cf. 677).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ξυστόν (spear-shaft, pole).

title: Patroclus leaves Eurypylus
greek: ἀγαθὴ δὲ παραίφασίς ἐστιν ἑταίρου (agathē de paraiphasis estin hetairou)
short: The narrative returns to Patroclus, left tending wounded Eurypylus since Book 11; seeing the wall fall, he runs to persuade Achilles. The Patrocleia begins.
body: At the end of Book 11 Achilles sent Patroclus to find out who was wounded. Nestor urged him to persuade Achilles to fight, or else to borrow his armour (11.794-803), and on his way back Patroclus stopped to treat Eurypylus' arrow-wound (11.809-48). The poet then left him there through four books of battle. Now he groans, slaps his thighs and runs, saying that 'a good thing is the persuasion of a comrade', which repeats Nestor's words at 11.793. Leaf points out that the timing is hard to fit with the events of Books 12-14 and suspects that lines were borrowed. Many readers value the technique all the same. Homer keeps one storyline waiting while another moves on, so that the moment Patroclus arrives in tears at Achilles' side (16.2-3) is exactly when the first ship catches fire.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XV (on 390-404) and note on 15.390.
Homer, Iliad 11.794-803 and 11.809-48 (Nestor's advice; Patroclus and Eurypylus).

title: The carpenter's line
greek: ὥς τε στάθμη δόρυ νήϊον ἐξιθύνει (hōs te stathmē dory nēion exithynei)
short: The battle is held dead level, like a ship's timber trued by a chalk-line in the hands of a craftsman taught by Athena.
body: The stathmē was a cord rubbed with chalk or red ochre and snapped against timber to mark a straight cutting line (LSJ). Odysseus uses one to build his raft (Od. 5.245). The image of a straight line expresses perfect balance: neither side can drive the other back. The craftsman 'well skilled in all manner of craft (sophiē) by the promptings of Athene' reflects Athena's role as patron of skilled work. She teaches shipbuilding at 5.60-1, and later she is honoured as Athena Ergane, 'the Worker'. Leaf notes that sophiē, the root of 'philosophy', appears only here in Homer, and he takes this as a sign that the passage is late. The ship's timber also fits the setting, since the fight is now around the ships themselves. Compare the evenly balanced fight likened to a woman's scales weighing wool at 12.433-5.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.412 (Athena as teacher of shipbuilding; σοφίη only here).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. στάθμη (carpenter's line; Il. 15.410).
Homer, Odyssey 5.245; Iliad 12.433-5.

title: Zeus breaks Teucer's bowstring
greek: ὅς οἱ ἐϋστρεφέα νευρὴν ... ῥῆξ' (hos hoi eustrephea neurēn ... rhēx')
short: As Teucer aims at Hector, Zeus snaps his new bowstring; the gods guard Hector until his appointed time.
body: Teucer, the half-brother of Telamonian Aias and the best Greek archer, carries a bow that Apollo gave him (15.440-1), and he has just shot Cleitus, son of Peisenor, the comrade of Polydamas, who was holding the reins of his chariot (15.445-7). When he takes aim at Hector himself, Zeus, 'who guarded Hector', breaks the 'well-twisted' string that Teucer had tied on only that morning. The arrow goes astray and the bow drops from his hand. Teucer sees that 'a god is utterly bringing to naught the counsels of our battle'. Aias tells him to take up a spear and shield instead, and he arms in the usual formulaic way (15.479-82). The scene repeats Book 8, where Hector stopped Teucer's archery by breaking his bowstring with a stone (8.324-9). Hector, for his part, reads the omen correctly: 'full easy to discern is the aid Zeus giveth to men' (15.490). The scene also shows how vulnerable an archer is, and why archery had lower status in heroic warfare.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.440-1 and 15.484-9.
Homer, Iliad 8.324-9 (Teucer's bowstring broken by Hector's stone).
Homer, Iliad 15.458-70 (Greek text).

anchor: die while fighting for his country
title: Dying for one's country
greek: οὔ οἱ ἀεικὲς ἀμυνομένῳ περὶ πάτρης τεθνάμεν (ou hoi aeikes amynomenōi peri patrēs tethnamen)
short: Hector's rallying cry, that it is no disgrace to die defending one's country if wife, children and land are saved, became a classic text of Greek patriotism.
body: Achaean heroes usually fight for personal glory, plunder and honour. Hector, defending a city, can appeal to something more communal. A man who falls 'defending his fatherland' (peri patrēs) has died without shame, because 'his wife is safe and his children after him, and his house and his portion of land'. The idea goes back to his rejection of omens at 12.243: 'one omen is best, to fight for one's country'. Later Greeks drew on these lines. The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus wrote that it is a fine thing for a good man to die fallen in the front rank fighting for his fatherland (fr. 10 West). In 330 BC the Athenian orator Lycurgus quoted Il. 15.494-9 in full to the jury in his speech Against Leocrates (103-4), as proof of how the ancestors valued courage. Horace's 'dulce et decorum est pro patria mori' (Odes 3.2.13) belongs to the same tradition, which Wilfred Owen bitterly questioned in 1917. Hector's words are moving, and also ironic: his own death will not save Troy.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), apparatus to 15.494-9 (readings of Lycurgus' quotation).

title: A guest-gift that saves a life
greek: ξεῖνος γάρ οἱ ἔδωκεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Εὐφήτης (xeinos gar hoi edōken anax andrōn Euphētēs)
short: Meges survives Dolops' spear because of a corselet his father Phyleus received as a guest-gift (xenia), an object with a history.
body: Homeric armour often has a story attached, and gifts between guest-friends (xenoi) bind families across generations. Phyleus, Meges' father, received this plated corselet from Euphetes, 'king of men', at Ephyre on the river Selleïs (compare 2.659), 'to wear in war, a defence against foe-men'. Now it protects his son. Guest-friendship (xenia) was a sacred, inherited bond protected by Zeus Xeinios: host and guest exchanged gifts, and the obligation passed to their descendants. That is why Diomedes and Glaucus refuse to fight in Book 6 and exchange armour instead (6.215-36). The gift here does what such bonds were meant to do, preserving the family of the man who received it. Leaf notes that the corselet with its gyala (plates) is mentioned in explicit terms, which is rare in Homer.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.529-31 (the corselet and its γύαλα).
Homer, Iliad 6.215-36 (Diomedes and Glaucus).

anchor: take ye shame in your hearts
title: Aidos: shame before one's comrades
greek: αἰδῶ θέσθ' ἐνὶ θυμῷ, ἀλλήλους τ' αἰδεῖσθε (aidō thesth' eni thymōi, allēlous t' aideisthe)
short: Aias tells the Greeks to feel aidos, shame before one another: men who feel it survive more often than they die, while runners win no glory.
body: Aidōs is the inhibiting sense of how one looks in others' eyes, between 'shame', 'respect' and 'conscience'. Aias' lines repeat Agamemnon's exhortation at 5.529-32. The practical argument is that soldiers who 'have shame each of the other' hold the line, so more of them live. Later in the book Nestor urges the same feeling, adding the thought of 'children and wife, of possessions and of his parents' (15.661-6). Shame and fear together keep the Greeks from scattering (15.657-8). The Trojans, by contrast, are urged on in Hector's speech by love of country (15.494-9). Aidōs is one of the poem's central social emotions. Hector feels it before the Trojan men and women (6.441-3, 22.105), and Achilles' loss of it in his treatment of Hector's corpse is what Apollo condemns in Book 24 (24.44-5).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. αἰδώς (reverence, awe; shame, sense of honour).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XV (on the stand at 515-91 and 592ff.).

title: Thetis' 'excessive' prayer
greek: Θέτιδος δ' ἐξαίσιον ἀρὴν πᾶσαν ἐπικρήνειε (Thetidos d' exaision arēn pasan epikrēneie)
short: The narrator reveals Zeus' timing: he waits only to see one Greek ship burn, fulfilling Thetis' prayer to the last, before turning the battle back.
body: The pivot of the whole plot is described here. Since Book 1 Zeus has granted Thetis' request to honour Achilles by letting the Trojans prevail (1.503-10). Now the narrator says he is waiting for 'the glare of a burning ship'. After that he will order the 'driving-back' (palōxis) of the Trojans. The adjective exaisios means 'beyond what is fitting or fated' (LSJ), and Murray renders it 'presumptuous'. Leaf observes that here 'the poet thus speaks explicitly as a Greek partisan'. Prophetic narrative of this kind is rare in Homer, and Leaf suspects lines 597-604 may have been added to remind listeners of the main plot. The passage also explains the strange rhythm of Books 15-16. Hector's triumph is real but limited in advance, and the fire he longs to bring (15.718) will set off the Greek counter-attack, the death of Patroclus and, in the end, his own death.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.596-604 and 15.598 (ἐξαίσιον, 'going beyond measure').
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἐξαίσιος ('beyond what is ordained'; Θέτιδος ἐ. ἀρήν, Il. 15.598).
Homer, Iliad 1.503-30 (Thetis' supplication and Zeus' nod).

anchor: brief was his span of life
title: Hector's frenzy and short life
greek: μινυνθάδιος γὰρ ἔμελλεν ἔσσεσθ' (minynthadios gar emellen essesth')
short: At the peak of his glory Hector rages like Ares, foaming at the mouth, while the narrator reminds us that Athena is already speeding his day of doom.
body: Hector at his height is compared to Ares and to a forest fire. 'Foam came forth about his mouth' (aphloismos, a word found only here in Homer), his eyes blaze, and his helmet shakes about his temples. He is close to the madness of battle that the poem elsewhere calls lyssa. Zeus honours him 'alone as he was amid so many', but the narrator immediately adds why: 'brief was his span of life to be', because Pallas Athena was already 'hastening on the day of his doom beneath the might of the son of Peleus'. The adjective minynthadios, 'short-lived', is the word Achilles uses of himself to his mother (1.352). Hector and Achilles are thus linked as men whose great moments come just before their deaths. Athena's role at Hector's actual death, when she deceives him in the likeness of Deiphobus (22.226-47), is foretold here.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἀφλοισμός ('foaming at the mouth', of an angry man, Il. 15.607).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. μινυνθάδιος (short-lived; Il. 1.352).

anchor: like a crag, sheer and great
title: Crag, wave and lion: a chain of similes
greek: ἠΰτε πέτρη ἠλίβατος μεγάλη (ēyte petrē ēlibatos megalē)
short: Three similes in quick succession: the Greeks stand like a sea-cliff, Hector falls on them like a wave on a ship, then like a lion among cattle.
body: Homer here piles similes together to slow the narrative at its most intense point. First the Greeks hold 'like a wall' (pyrgēdon), like a huge sea-cliff that withstands winds and swelling waves. Then the image is reversed. Hector, 'shining all about as with fire', crashes on them like a wave on a swift ship, and the sailors are only a little way from death, a fitting image for men fighting at their ships. Finally he is a lion attacking cattle in a marsh, guarded by an inexperienced herdsman who keeps to the front and back of the herd while the lion takes a heifer from the middle. Leaf calls this last simile 'two-sided', beginning with one comparison and developing another out of the same picture. Together the three pictures show the Greek defence first holding and then breaking.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.618, 15.621, 15.629-36.
Homer, Iliad 15.618-37 (Greek text).

title: Periphetes, son of Copreus
greek: Κοπρῆος φίλον υἱόν (Koprēos philon huion)
short: The one Mycenaean warrior Hector kills here is the son of Copreus, the herald who carried Eurystheus' orders to Heracles. His name means 'Dung-man'.
body: Copreus (from kopros, 'dung') was the go-between used by King Eurystheus to give Heracles his labours. The story was that Eurystheus was so afraid of Heracles that he hid in a bronze jar sunk in the ground and sent commands through his herald (Apollodorus 2.5.1). Copreus appears in this role in Euripides' Heraclidae. Leaf calls Copreus 'evidently a name invented to express contempt'. Homer turns the old story into a moral contrast: 'of a father baser by far was begotten a son goodlier in all manner of excellence (aretē)'. Periphetes dies by bad luck. Turning to retreat, he trips on the rim of his own body-length shield and falls on his back, and Hector spears him. Leaf notes that he is the only Mycenaean named as fighting in the Iliad.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.639-45.

anchor: shield that reached to the feet
title: The body-length shield
greek: ποδηνεκέ' ἕρκος ἀκόντων (podēneke' herkos akontōn)
short: Periphetes trips on a shield 'reaching to the feet', a type of shield older than the round shield of most Homeric fighting.
body: Homer describes two kinds of shield without clearly distinguishing them. The usual one is round and bossed, held on the forearm. But some heroes carry a huge body-shield: Aias' 'tower-like' shield (7.219), and Hector's, whose rim knocks against his neck and ankles as he walks (6.117-18). That was the shield of the Mycenaean age, a figure-of-eight or tower shape of layered ox-hide hung from a shoulder strap (telamōn), known from the Lion Hunt dagger from Mycenae and other finds. Periphetes' podēnekēs shield, 'reaching to the foot' (LSJ), belongs to this type, and its bulk is what trips him. The passage is one of several in the poem where memories of Bronze Age equipment survive inside a later poetic tradition. Leaf discusses the hard verb palto ('tripped') here and the strap that would be needed for such a shield.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ποδηνεκής ('reaching down to the foot'; ἀσπίς Il. 15.646).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.645 (πάλτο) and on 16.803 (the τελαμών of the older shield).

title: Aias as a trick-rider
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἀνὴρ ἵπποισι κελητίζειν ἐῢ εἰδώς (hōs d' hot' anēr hippoisi kelētizein eü eidōs)
short: Aias strides from deck to deck like a performer who leaps from horse to horse of a galloping team as crowds watch on the road to the city.
body: Aias, wielding a 22-cubit pike, keeps moving across the decks of the beached ships, and the poet compares him to a skilled rider who yokes four picked horses, drives them along a public road towards a city, and jumps from one to another at full speed while men and women admire him. LSJ glosses kelētizein as riding, 'of one who leaps from horse to horse'. Aristarchus noted that Homer knows horse-riding but never puts his heroes on horseback in the narrative; the trumpet, too, appears only in similes. Leaf takes this to mean the poet was aware that such things were recent and did not belong to the heroic age. The simile therefore brings the audience's own world, with its riders and festival crowds, into the battle. It conveys Aias' agility, balance and visibility, and the steadiness of a man the Greeks rely on.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 15.679-80 (Aristarchus on riding and the trumpet).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. κελητίζω (Il. 15.679).

title: The ship of Protesilaus
greek: ἣ Πρωτεσίλαον ἔνεικεν ἐς Τροίην, οὐδ' αὖτις ἀπήγαγε (hē Prōtesilaon eneiken es Troiēn, oud' autis apēgage)
short: Hector seizes the stern of Protesilaus' ship. It carried to Troy the first Greek to die there and never took him home.
body: Protesilaus was the first Achaean to leap ashore at Troy and the first to be killed, leaving a widow with her cheeks torn in mourning and a house half-built (2.698-702). His ship is mentioned first at 13.681, and Leaf notes that it becomes central in the fighting at the end of Book 15. It is the ship that Hector holds and Aias defends, and at 16.122-3 it is the first to be set on fire. The detail that it 'brought him not back again to his native land' turns a ship into a reminder of failed homecoming (nostos), the hope the Greeks are now close to losing for good: if the ships burn, no one goes home. Later legend gave Protesilaus a famous afterlife: his wife Laodamia's grief brought him back from the dead for three hours, a story later retold by Wordsworth in 'Laodamia'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 13.681 and 15.705.
Homer, Iliad 2.698-702 (Protesilaus' death).
Homer, Iliad 16.122-3 (the first ship fired).

title: The aphlaston (stern ornament)
greek: ἄφλαστον μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων (aphlaston meta chersin echōn)
short: Murray's 'ensign' is the aphlaston, the curved ornamental tip of a ship's stern, which Hector grips and will not let go.
body: The aphlaston (Latin aplustre) was the upward-curving stern-post of a ship with its decoration (LSJ: 'curved poop of a ship with its ornaments'). The word occurs only here in Homer. To grip it was to claim the ship. Leaf compares Herodotus' account of Marathon, where the Athenian Cynegeirus, brother of Aeschylus, grabbed the aphlasta of a Persian ship and had his hand cut off with an axe (Hdt. 6.114). Hector's refusal to let go turns the stern into a symbol of victory, and he calls for fire, describing this day as 'recompense for all' the suffering the ships have brought. In later Greek art the aphlaston was carried home as a trophy of naval victory. Hector's grip is the furthest point of the Trojan advance in the poem.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἄφλαστον ('curved poop of a ship with its ornaments', Il. 15.717; Hdt. 6.114).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.716-17 (ἄφλαστον only here; Herodotus 6.114).
Herodotus 6.114 (Cynegeirus at Marathon).

title: Hector blames the elders
greek: κακότητι γερόντων (kakotēti gerontōn)
short: Hector claims the Trojan elders had always held him back from attacking the ships; Leaf notes this excuse appears nowhere else.
body: In his moment of triumph Hector explains Troy's years of defensive fighting: the Trojan elders (gerontes, the city's council, like the old men on the wall at 3.149) kept him from attacking the Greek ships out of 'cowardice' (kakotēs). Leaf points out that there is 'no hint elsewhere of such an excuse'. In Book 9 Achilles gives a different reason, that Hector never dared go beyond the Scaean gates while Achilles was fighting (9.352-5). Hector's claim reveals his character. He is confident and quick to blame others, and he believes that Zeus, who once 'dulled our wits', now drives him on. The poem soon shows the danger of that confidence. In Book 18 he will overrule the cautious Polydamas, and in Book 22 he admits that 'I destroyed the people by my recklessness' (22.104).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.721 (γερόντων = councillors; no hint elsewhere of this excuse).

title: The seven-foot bench
greek: θρῆνυν ἐφ' ἑπταπόδην (thrēnyn eph' heptapodēn)
short: Driven off the deck, Aias falls back to a 'seven-foot bench', probably the helmsman's bench or a raised plank, and from there spears twelve fire-bearers.
body: A thrēnys is normally a footstool (14.240). LSJ explains the 'seven-foot thrēnys' here as 'perhaps the helmsman's bench or bridge', and Murray translates it as 'bridge'. The exact part of the ship cannot be identified. What matters is that Aias has had to give up the deck (ikria) under the hail of missiles, while still keeping the fire away. His last speech is grim. There is no city wall behind them and no allies; they are pinned on the Trojan plain 'with naught to support us but the sea', and so 'in the might of our hands is the light of deliverance'. The book ends with a precise number, twelve men wounded in front of the ships, which reads like a record of one man's last defence. The next book takes up exactly this scene (16.101-23), when Hector cuts Aias' spear in two and the ship catches fire.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. θρῆνυς ('the seven-foot bench, perh. helmsman's bench or bridge', Il. 15.729).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 15.729 (ἑπταπόδην).
Homer, Iliad 16.101-23 (Aias overwhelmed; the ship fired).
